notes.h: Background and causes: what a Eucharistic Congress is and why Dublin
notes.b: The Eucharistic Congress was an international Catholic gathering held in Dublin in 1932. Its date was chosen to tie Catholicism to Irish identity, and it came ten years after independence, in a country where the Church was very strong.
points: An International Eucharistic Congress is a gathering of Catholics from many countries to honour the Eucharist, the sacrament in which Catholics believe bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. The first was held in 1881, and each is held in a different city.

Dublin's was the 31st Congress. 1932 was chosen because it was the 1,500th anniversary of the traditional date of St Patrick's arrival in Ireland in 432, which linked the event to Irish Catholic identity.

The invitation and the early planning were made while Cosgrave's government (Cumann na nGaedheal, in office 1922-32) was in power, so the Congress was planned under Cosgrave. The Church and the state treated it as a national occasion.
Archbishop Edward Byrne of Dublin headed the organising effort, and the Pope sent a legate (a personal representative), Cardinal Lorenzo Lauri.
The Free State was ten years old in 1932, after the Treaty and the Civil War, so the Congress was an opportunity for the new state to show itself to the world.

The Catholic Church had a strong position in Irish life because the vast majority of the population was Catholic and the Church ran most schools and many hospitals. This is why a religious event could become a national one.
notes.tip: For short questions on cause and context, the answers are: why Dublin and why 1932 (the Patrick anniversary), who organised it (Archbishop Byrne) and who represented the Pope (Cardinal Lauri).

notes.h: Preparations and the change of government
notes.b: The Congress was planned under Cosgrave but held under de Valera, whose Fianna Fáil party took office three months before it opened. Both governments backed it, and the preparations were large.
points: Fianna Fáil won the February 1932 election and de Valera became President of the Executive Council (head of government) on 9 March 1932, three months before the Congress.
De Valera was known for his personal piety, so he took a leading part and his government gave the planning full support. He did not issue the invitation, which had come from Cosgrave's government.
Dublin was prepared with altars, decorations, flags and illuminations, and the streets of poorer districts (the slums) were decorated too, so that the whole city took part.
A large altar was built in the Phoenix Park for the final Mass, and the arrangements for transport, accommodation and crowd control were extensive because very large crowds were expected.

A radio station at Athlone was brought into use in 1932, so that the ceremonies and the Pope's message could reach listeners around the country. A loudspeaker system let the huge crowds hear the services.
Visitors came from the United States, Britain and Europe, and thousands of pilgrims came from Northern Ireland.
A national committee raised money by public subscription (donations from the public), and parishes organised local groups for the processions.
Thousands of volunteers acted as stewards, and special first-aid and catering services were arranged for the Phoenix Park.
notes.tip: Planned under Cosgrave, held under de Valera: do not credit de Valera with the invitation. Cosgrave's supporters complained that Fianna Fáil got the credit.

notes.b: The Congress showed close co-operation between the Catholic hierarchy (the bishops) and the new Fianna Fáil government. It also exposed the unresolved question of the Crown's representative in the Free State.
points: Cardinal Lauri arrived at Dún Laoghaire on 21 June 1932, the day before the Congress opened. De Valera and Archbishop Byrne welcomed him, and he was escorted through crowds to Dublin.

The Governor-General, James McNeill, who represented the Crown in the Free State, was not invited to the legate's reception at Dublin Castle. The Crown and the oath were live issues for the new government, so this was a deliberate snub.
The affair was part of the conflict that ended in McNeill's dismissal on 1 November 1932, after the government advised the King to remove him.
De Valera used the occasion to present his government as both Catholic and independent of the Crown. In this way the dispute showed sovereignty, the state's independent standing, being asserted.
The Congress also gave de Valera's new government a chance to show that it could work with the Church.
notes.tip: The Governor-General snub earns credit under sovereignty. Keep the dates distinct: 21 June is the legate's arrival, while the Congress itself ran 22-26 June.

notes.b: Five days of Masses, processions and services culminated in an open-air Mass in the Phoenix Park and a procession to O'Connell Bridge. Remember the dates, since examiners reward dated detail.
points: The Congress ran from 22 to 26 June 1932 and opened at the Pro-Cathedral in Dublin, with Masses and services in city churches, including a procession of the Blessed Sacrament (the consecrated bread of the Eucharist).
On 25 June a children's Mass was held in the Phoenix Park, attended by about 100,000 children.

On Sunday 26 June the closing Mass was celebrated at the altar in the Phoenix Park before a crowd often estimated at about a million. This may be exaggerated, but it is described as about a quarter of the population of the state.
John McCormack, the famous Irish tenor, sang César Franck's Panis Angelicus at a Mass of the Congress.
A message from Pope Pius XI was broadcast live by radio from the Vatican to the crowd, so the Pope could address the people of Ireland without being present.
After the Mass a procession went from the park to O'Connell Bridge, where Cardinal Lauri gave the closing benediction (a final blessing) to a very large crowd, up to several hundred thousand people.
Cardinal Lauri addressed the crowds and presided as the Pope's representative throughout the Congress.
notes.tip: A 100-mark essay needs dated detail: 22-26 June, the children's Mass, the closing Mass, McCormack, the radio message and O'Connell Bridge. Say 'often estimated' for the crowd, and name McCormack's piece only as sung at a Mass of the Congress, with no date.

notes.h: Organisation, media and the image of the Free State
notes.b: The size of the event tested the state's administration and brought international attention. Its success helped present the Free State as a stable and devout country.
points: Special trains, buses and sailings brought crowds from all over Ireland and abroad, and the Garda and the Army managed the crowds.
Loudspeakers allowed huge crowds to hear the ceremonies, and radio carried the broadcast to the country, so people who could not be in the Phoenix Park could still take part.
Foreign newspapers reported the event, and it gave the Free State international publicity as a devout, stable Catholic country.
The Congress passed off without major disorder, which was a strong demonstration of public order only ten years after the Civil War.
The event was a success for de Valera, whose prestige grew at home and abroad.
Archbishop Byrne and the organising committee had to coordinate bishops from around the world, and papal flags and Irish flags were flown together.
The state radio service, which grew from the Athlone station brought into use for the Congress, was named Radio Éireann in 1938.
notes.tip: Examiners reward the image abroad as one named strand of significance. Back it with evidence such as foreign press attention, order kept ten years after the Civil War, and radio.

notes.b: In the North the Congress was seen very differently. It highlighted the religious divide on the island, since unionists (who wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom) saw it as a threat.
points: Catholic pilgrims travelling by train and bus to and from Dublin were attacked in Northern Ireland, and trains were stoned at places such as Portadown, Lisburn and Belfast.
Police made baton charges at some stations to protect pilgrims.
Unionists saw the Congress as proof that the Free State was a Catholic state, which reinforced their support for partition (the division of the island) because they feared Rome rule.
Protestant newspapers and Orange leaders criticised the scale of Catholic display, and the attacks on pilgrims added to sectarian tension.
For Northern nationalists, the Congress was a source of pride and reinforced their sense of belonging to an Irish Catholic nation.
notes.tip: The attacks on pilgrims earn credit under unionist perceptions. Name places such as Portadown and Belfast.

notes.b: The Congress is usually assessed through four themes: Church-state relations, Catholic identity, Ireland's image and standing abroad, and unionist perceptions. Naming each and giving evidence earns credit, whereas narrative alone does not.
points: Church and state: it showed the alliance between the hierarchy and the political leadership, the same alignment that is seen in the tone of the 1937 constitution and in social legislation. The Congress passed no laws and did not cause the constitution.

Catholic identity: it presented Ireland as a Catholic nation, in line with the Gaelic and Catholic ideal of the 1930s. This is an example of conformity, the pressure to share the dominant Catholic values, as censorship laws of the period were too.
International image: it presented the Free State as stable, devout and independent, and made de Valera well known abroad.
Sovereignty: the Governor-General dispute showed the government's desire to downgrade the Crown's representative and assert the state's independent standing.
Unionist view: it confirmed fears of a state dominated by the Catholic Church.
Contemporary view: the Catholic press and most of the public regarded it as a great national triumph.
Later view: historians describe it as the high point of the Church's public influence, and a sign of the conformity that marked the 1930s. Some stress it as a political success for de Valera.
De Valera's critics in Cumann na nGaedheal noted that the Congress had been planned by Cosgrave's government but that Fianna Fáil gained the credit.
notes.tip: The key conclusion for the 2015 document-based question and for essays is that the significance was symbolic rather than legal. Place documents in context: planning under Cosgrave, the change of government, the legate and the Phoenix Park Mass.

notes.b: The Congress was a great public success, but its effect was largely symbolic. Examiners reward judgements set out as paired points.
points: Achievement: it showed the state could organise a major international event soon after the Civil War.
Achievement: it united people across party lines at a time of political change.
Limit: it did not change any laws or institutions, so its influence was cultural and political rather than legal.
Limit: it deepened the distrust between North and South, and Catholic and Protestant, on the island.
Contemporary view: a triumph for the Church and the nation.
Later view: a moment when church, state and nation appeared identical, which later generations judged more critically.
notes.tip: Pair achievements with limits, and contemporary views with later views. A clear thesis (a symbolic success, the high point of the Church-state alliance) earns marks.

keyTerms.definition: An international Catholic gathering to honour the Eucharist; the 31st was held in Dublin on 22–26 June 1932.
The Catholic sacrament in which bread and wine are believed to become the body and blood of Christ.
The Pope's personal representative at the Congress, Cardinal Lorenzo Lauri.
The pressure to share the dominant Catholic values of the state, expressed in events such as the Congress.
The Free State's independent standing, shown by its international profile and by the dispute over the Governor-General.
The close understanding between the Catholic hierarchy and the government in the 1930s.
The closing open-air Mass on 26 June 1932, attended by hundreds of thousands.
The Crown's representative in the Free State, James McNeill in 1932, who was snubbed during the Congress.
